topic_title: The Confession Arizona Chose to Protect

slides.headline: A Bishop Knew. He Said Nothing.
slides.body: Arizona's Supreme Court just ruled he never had to. The church decides what counts as confession — not the law.

slides.headline: Bisbee, 2011: A Father Confesses
slides.body: Paul Adams, a Border Patrol agent, told his LDS bishop he was abusing his 5-year-old daughter. Bishop John Herrod stayed silent.

slides.headline: He Confessed Again. And Again.
slides.body: 2012, 2013: Adams repeated the confession to church leaders. In 2013 bishops excommunicated him and still called no police.

slides.headline: Homeland Security Found Her First
slides.body: Abuse lasted six years before a 2017 federal investigation exposed it — the church had known since 2011.

slides.headline: The Law Lets Faith Decide
slides.body: Arizona's court ruled churches, not judges, define what counts as a protected confession. Thirty states still shield clergy this way.

slides.headline: Whose Silence Does the Law Protect?
slides.body: A father confessed three times. Every time, the church chose secrecy over a child. The court just called that legal.
